slides.t: Thank you. I will report our technique for the short-scar deep-plane facelift and our experience with the first 10 patients.
I have no conflicts of interest to disclose.

The deep-plane facelift is a highly effective procedure, but it is sometimes avoided because of the length of the incision. (click) We therefore performed an incisional facelift with deep-plane dissection through a short incision from in front of the ear to behind the ear, and we report it here.
This is the technique. We enter through a small incision around the ear.
As shown, the skin is incised from in front of the ear to behind the ear,
and after subcutaneous undermining over this area,
we set the entry line into the deep plane as a zigzag rather than a straight line. (click) This design follows the bucket handle modification reported by Abraham and colleagues.

This is the deep-plane entry after subcutaneous undermining. (click)
The design is intended to secure a wide deep operative field and dissection area while keeping the incision short.

In the deep plane, we dissect three spaces. (click) The premasseteric space and the sub-platysmal plane are loose layers that can be dissected safely even through a short incision. (click) On the SCM fascia, we cut and release the ligaments between the fascia and the platysma.
This is dissection of the premasseteric space. Here is the video. This is a very loose layer, and with a blunt dissecting instrument we can sometimes easily reach the side of the mouth.

Next is dissection on the SCM fascia. (click) Posteriorly, the external jugular vein and the great auricular nerve appear, and we preserve them. Thorough dissection here makes it easier to define the jawline.

(click) (click) We bluntly dissect the first and second spaces, (click) and then divide the cord-like tissue left between them, the cervical retaining ligaments. The idea of dissecting the easier spaces first and connecting them afterward is based on the Caves maneuver of Martins and colleagues.
Because the dissection plane is already established in the first and second spaces, dissecting the remaining tissue relatively superficially, just beneath the platysma, makes this a very safe step.
(click) This is the extent of dissection: to the marionette line, and in the neck 3-4 cm caudal to the mandibular border. (click) The buccal fat can also be drawn out and sutured upward.
The SMAS is fixed (click) to the mastoid periosteum, following the mastoid crevasse of Talei and colleagues. The rest of the SMAS is fixed to the deep conchal cartilage.
The subjects were the first 10 patients, all women aged 42 to 64 years. Buccal and submandibular liposuction was performed in all cases, and we evaluated facial contour and complications.

These are the results, including complications. Over a mean follow-up of 6 months, there were no hematomas and no injuries to the facial nerve or the great auricular nerve. One patient required revision, for a retroauricular dog-ear. Improvements in the mandibular border and the neck contour were both good.

Case 1: a 59-year-old woman, before and 6 months after surgery. On the frontal view, the marionette lines improved, and the irregularity of the mandibular contour also improved. On the lateral view, the neck and submandibular lines have become well defined.
Case 2: a 64-year-old woman. The contour from the jawline to the neck has become straight.
Cases 3 and 4: women aged 59 and 61. In both, the neck and submandibular contours improved on the lateral view.

This is a comparison with previous short-incision techniques. The MACS lift and the method of Baker and colleagues rely mainly on plication or excision of the SMAS, not on the deep plane. A deep-plane technique through a short incision is the MADE lift of Jacono and colleagues. Our technique differs in that, through the same short incision, we dissect onto the SCM fascia in the neck and fix to the mastoid periosteum.

Some may point out that a short incision gives a narrow and risky operative field. The zigzag entry is designed to widen the operative field, and because dissection starts in the loose layers, it can be started safely even through a short incision.

In conclusion, we consider the short-scar deep-plane facelift with a zigzag incision to be a refinement that can combine safety, the reliability of the deep-plane technique, and an effect on the neck. Long-term results and evaluation of cases treated with this technique alone are future tasks. Thank you for your attention.
